Liver!!! You're joking, right? Sorry, all the liver-lovers, I can't stand the stuff!

Anyway, projects for near future (hah!):

rehalogenating dead plates

colour control in DCG and Silver. I have an idea for improving colour rendition. I ain't saying too much, but while idling in an opticians waiting room, the following thought experiment occurred to me:

Embedd three LEDs, say "red", "green" and "blue", into an object (the door of the waiting room, eg), control the currents such that the LEDS colour become so similar to that of the object that the individual LEDS become invisible. Now remove the LEDS from the object, turn them around and shine all three of them back onto the object. Will the resulting light from the LEDS be visible on the surface of the object?

A mathematical description of continuously varying holographic aberrations ( a suggestion from Colin took me down a new path I had not considered)

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md:
I think 'yes', the light from the LEDs will be visible on the object. It's a pretty good guess, since there's probably many ways that the light from the LEDs would be visible, and only a few (or one) way it would not be visible.

Here are two arguments:

1. The object is illuminated by some source illumination, say a flourescent bulb in the ceiling. The source illumination has some spectral energy response - energy versus frequency. The object also has its own spectral reflectivity response. The actual light being reflected off the object is the product of the two responses. By your experiment, this is also the same response (as perceived by your eyes) from the LEDs. But when you illuminate the object with the LEDs, the response would be the product of the object reflectivity response and the LEDs, which are (to your eyes) equal to the product of the illumination response (the bulb in the ceiling) and the object reflectivity response. So I argue the net result would include the effect of the object reflectivity response twice, and therefore not be identical.

2. On a pure energy level, there would be more energy coming from the object if it was illuminated by both the source (flourescent bulb) and the LEDs, than by the source alone. (You didn't specify if you turned off the bulb in the ceiling for the second part of the experiment).

 There, inside, you filter and apportion

 you separate and divide,

 you multiply and lubricate

 you raise and gather

 the threads and the grams of life...

 from you I hope for justice:

 I love life: Do not betray me! Work on!

 Do not arrest my song.

I kind of like liver. With onions, sometimes. 

"Rehalogenating dead plates"- now that sounds useful, especially when extended to erasing and rehalogenating dud plates. I wonder if it's possible to restore an exposed and bleached plate (where no silver loss has occurred) to its pristine state? The other question being how best to re-activate the plate. Ascorbic acid sort of works, but I suspect ammonia might be better.
